output.headline: Burnham unveils new help-to-buy scheme as he vows to deliver radical change
output.bodyHtml:
Andy Burnham has said he can deliver on his promise of radical change for the country despite severe economic headwinds, telling the Guardian: “There’s always things you can do; it’s just whether you’re prepared to do them.”

The prime minister said delivering fiscal stability would be “crucial” so that the government could focus on fixing bigger problems, though he acknowledged public finances were “challenging” ahead of next month’s budget.

A series of global economic shocks, including the Iran conflict, has put the UK economy under intense inflationary pressure and pushed up borrowing costs, leaving the government limited room for manoeuvre.

Related: Andy Burnham announces new homes scheme for first-time buyers

Ahead of his first Labour conference as prime minister, however, Burnham sought to reassure voters he was willing to make tough decisions to deliver change and show the markets he could ensure fiscal stability while preparing the groundwork for more substantial change ahead.

Speaking to the Guardian on the eve of his first conference as Labour leader, he said: “The public would have more respect for us if we go and grab something difficult … and say, ‘Right, we’re going to do something here’, rather than constantly playing the political game before fixing the problems.

“It’s challenging, definitely, but there are still things that you can do. Always in politics, there are things that you can do. The question is sometimes: Are you prepared to do them? Yeah, I am prepared to do them.”

When asked about the need for a large fiscal buffer against shocks, he said the key thing was stability, indicating that he understood the need to reassure the markets, but that more radical transformation of the state would follow.

“I do think it is crucial to have stability and to show that there’s a willingness to face up to the reality of some of these difficult things. But actually from that stability, the permission can come to make bigger change that, in the end, could put the country in a stronger position in relation to the public finances,” he said.

“You have to have stability, but you have to do what you can within that. You can’t pursue a major programme of change, which is what I believe the country needs, in a chaotic situation.”

After ruling out holding a snap general election before 2029, Burnham said he wanted to set out a clear path for how the country could move to a better place – and that he hadn’t been spending his time “sitting politicking and strategising” but instead was focused on fixing problems.

His ambition to give people “a bit more belief that things can improve” across the country, he said, would not come from “endlessly running elections and referendums”.

He denied having had discussions with his senior team about whether to call an early election. “The speculation in no way matches the internal discussion because there isn’t one,” he said, rejecting claims he did not have a mandate as the public had voted for the Labour party.

However, Burnham acknowledged he was hemmed in on tax and the fiscal rules of Keir Starmer’s manifesto commitments, and suggested he would have done it differently had he been in charge at the time.

“I’ve inherited those positions and, as I say, I think the main thing for me is to focus on the here and now for people, not to be self-serving about ‘oh, what would suit me?’ and playing politics. That’s not where my mind is, and possibly would have framed it different, but we are where we are, you know, and that’s the reality.”

Burnham pointed to measures already taken to help with energy bills, with VAT on electricity due to be scrapped from next week, as he played down speculation that Labour may offer more support with the price cap set to soar from January. “I think people need to remember that measures have already been taken,” he said.

The prime minister also reiterated that while he thought the welfare bill was too high, the will among Labour MPs was “not there for crude cuts” because they would push people into crisis, so a longer-term approach to reform was required.

Having set out both the risks and the opportunities of artificial intelligence at the UN last week, Burnham said he was concerned about rogue AI agents attacking state institutions in the UK, after Australia’s medicare system was hit.

Related: The tricky tests awaiting Andy Burnham after Labour conference

Burnham addressed the presence of far-right protesters on the streets of Britain, accusing Daniel Thomas, who has led black-clad anti-migrant vigilantes on the streets of some English towns, of “creating fear” but did not go as far as Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, who accused him of being an “outright racist”.

Speaking of Thomas’s masked gangs, he said: “I mean that’s not Britain. That’s not what we want to see in people’s communities. There’s legitimate concerns about issues, and then there is intimidation – and that is intimidation,” he said.

The prime minister also addressed political funding, which has been in the spotlight since Reform UK received two record-breaking £36m donations from cryptocurrency billionaires, saying that – contrary to reports – he would not rule out a domestic donations cap.

“You know I think we do need to continue to have a cross-party discussion about how do we uphold trust in politics? How do we not give the impression that politics can be bought and that people are, if you like, unduly influenced?”

He was also open to looking at election spending limits, he said, which are now being examined by the Electoral Commission, adding that he has “real concerns” about crypto-fuelled politics.

An emotional Burnham revealed that the death of his father, Roy, last week had made him more determined to deliver. “I’m in this job for what I can do for people, not for what it can do for me … to make the changes that my dad, for instance, long pushed me to make,” he said.

“It’s been a hard thing, if I’m honest, coming into this position in the last three months when I also knew in my heart that I was starting this journey as my dad was ending his.

Related: From idealists to struggling sceptics: how Labour’s majority depends on five progressive voter types – in charts

“Although that’s hard, and I’m not seeking sympathy in saying it, I say it because the coming together of those two things increases my determination to make a difference on the things that I’ve long said I want to fix.”

With political courage expected to be a focus of his speech to Labour’s conference in Liverpool, Burnham said he was willing to be honest with the public about what needed to happen, even if it was difficult to hear.

“I think the public want to see, number one, honesty about things. So not spin or putting things a certain way that’s self-serving. They want honesty, and then they want, I think, difficult but real decisions,” said Burnham.

“Not difficult decisions and making a fetish out of that, but actually grasping nettles and then moving things forward. I don’t think politics has been prepared to do that enough in recent times.”

Burnham criticised previous governments for failing to tackle difficult issues such as social care, housing supply and youth unemployment, saying longer-term reform was needed because there were no “easy or quick wins”.

He revealed there would be a new help-to-buy scheme aimed at giving first-time buyers who cannot rely on the “bank of mum and dad” the keys to their own home. It will be funded by reallocating existing budgets, although it is unclear which ones, rather than through extra borrowing.

Burnham also said he wanted to deliver significant progress on social care reform – a manifesto commitment – before the next election. “Who is going to do something to actually make it real? I’m saying to you that I am going to address this directly.”
output.standfirst: Exclusive: the prime minister unveils a new help-to-buy scheme and vows to press ahead with radical change, despite public finances he calls ‘challenging’ amid global economic shocks pushing up inflation and borrowing costs.
output.progress: Burnham is funding a new help-to-buy scheme for first-time buyers and has not ruled out a cap on political donations.

output.headline: Northern Ireland leaders urge calm as courts settle parade dispute
output.bodyHtml:
A loyalist parade through a nationalist street in the Northern Ireland town of Portadown will go ahead under a fresh set of restrictions, for the first time in nearly 30 years, after courts overturned a ban late on Saturday night.

The Parades Commission placed a number of restrictions on the procession, including an 8am start and limiting the number of participants to 35 people, but did not impose any restrictions on the route.

On Friday night, the British prime minister, Andy Burnham, appealed to leaders to “work calmly” through the weekend while the Northern Ireland secretary, Chris Bryant, called for “cool heads”, saying Northern Ireland had “withstood many moments of sharp disagreement over the years” and must do so again.

A request to the commission for permission for a countermarch, initially estimated by the court to draw as many as 5,000 people, was later revised down to 300, after fears of clashes had increased on Saturday.

Amid concerns the march could lead to fresh sectarian violence, the Orange Order parade down the Garvaghy Road is due to take place at 8am on Sunday morning, following a legal back-and-forth in recent days.

Justice Patricia Smyth had earlier issued an order temporarily suspending the parade, after a five-hour hearing at a special sitting of the high court on Saturday.

Smyth had urged all sides to “step back from the abyss” and take responsible decisions for “the sake of everyone in Northern Ireland”.

Before her ruling, Smyth had asked the parties in court, including the Police Service of Northern Ireland and the Parades Commission, to “consider carefully the very important issues to our society” raised in this case, and the importance that they were dealt with properly given the “importance of this case to community relations”.

She also noted that the issues of judicial review were of “such fundamental importance” that it could be unwise to hold a full hearing without all the facts.

Smyth had warned on Saturday that “this particular long-running dispute has the potential to escalate within Northern Ireland”.

“Be big enough to step back from the abyss,” she had told the parties in court.

Lady Chief Justice Siobhan Keegan, at a sitting of the court of appeals at 11.30pm on Saturday, said the high court judge who granted the injunction against the march had “unfortunately erred in law”.

A new application at the high court to stop the Protestant protest from passing through the Catholic area was also dismissed in the early hours of Sunday morning.

Justice Michael Humphreys heard the time-limited sitting, which began at 12.20am on Sunday.

He acknowledged the “unusual if not unprecedented circumstances as it is now 1.45am, with a parade scheduled to begin in just over six hours’ time”.

Outlining his decision, Humphreys cited case law that as a public body the courts must respect its judgment and “their decisions will not be lightly interfered with”.

“The picture painted here is of a public body which took evidence from the relevant sources, weighed up the key issues which were in play and arrived at a reasoned decision,” he said.

“The jurisdiction to impugn (a) public body’s decision on that basis is necessarily limited to cases where no reasonable decision could arrive at that outcome and in my view in this case that threshold has not been met.”

The march down Garvaghy Road had been banned for 28 years due to widespread sectarian violence in 1998 outside Drumcree church.

Michelle O’Neill, first minister of Northern Ireland, said after the appeal decision late on Saturday: “The decision tonight to overturn the court ruling, and force an unwanted orange march through the Garvaghy Road, is disgraceful.

“This march is steeped in a history of hate, sectarian violence, and murder, and championed by Unionist leaders.

“Our message tonight is clear. There is no going back. Not tomorrow. Not ever. Sinn Féin stands fully with the Garvaghy Road community, and they have the full support of people from right across Ireland in the period ahead.”

The SDLP leader, Claire Hanna, said the parade plan was “provocative”. She told residents she was “so sorry” that some “bad faith actors” were “intent on reopening the hurt and the traumas of the past”.

The Democratic Unionist MP Carla Lockhart insisted nationalist residents on the road had “nothing to fear” from the march on Sunday, but Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald described the decision as “utterly reckless”.
output.standfirst: Political leaders urged calm and the Parades Commission capped numbers at 35, after courts overturned the 28-year ban on the Orange Order’s Garvaghy Road march, which Sinn Féin’s Michelle O’Neill called ‘disgraceful’.
output.progress: Political leaders are urging calm and the Parades Commission has restricted the parade to 35 people with an 8am start.

output.headline: Iran says it remains ready to negotiate over Hormuz deal
output.bodyHtml:
Iran has proposed reopening the strait of Hormuz within a week and resuming nuclear talks, in return for the lifting of the US naval blockade of Iranian ports. But US president Donald Trump has said he has rejected the proposal.

“They made a proposal but I reject it,” he told reporters at the White House.

After a meeting with the UN secretary general, António Guterres, the Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, said: “Iran has not walked away from the negotiating table, but given past experiences, it no longer trusts the United States.”

In an interview with the CBS show Face the Nation, Pezeshkian said Tehran was ready for talks on its nuclear programme and other issues, but would not accept “bullying or coercion”.

“Iran is not seeking war, but will defend itself against pressure, threats and attacks,” Pezeshkian said, adding that it had already agreed that “we’re not supposed to develop nuclear weapons”.

A US official had earlier said discussions with Iran through mediators were “positive and constructive” and, on Friday, Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, detailed the proposal to reporters outside the UN security council.

Araghchi said late on Saturday that Tehran had seen an initial reaction from Trump to its proposal but had yet to receive a response through mediators.

Iran was waiting for the mediators to convey the definitive US position and would make a decision based on it, he added.

During a three-hour meeting at the UN general assembly in New York earlier this week, Iran had proposed reopening the strait, which would have relieved pressure on global energy markets, and restarting talks on its nuclear programme within seven days.

In return, as well as lifting its naval blockade, Iran wants the US to permit the release of some of Iran’s frozen assets, restore the waiver that lifted sanctions on Iran’s oil exports and observe a “ceasefire on all fronts”.

That would involve the US president convincing Israel to end its attacks on Iran-backed Hezbollah in Lebanon, a tall order, and allowing the strait to reopen largely on Iran’s terms, with the new route predominantly going through Iranian waters.

Saudi Arabia is also said to be concerned that the route deal is bilateral between Iran and Oman, and not with the Gulf states as joint signatories.

Araghchi said the seven-day timeline to open the strait and resume talks could start as soon as the US accepts Iran’s proposal. The initial steps would take about four to five days to complete, the strait would be opened on the sixth day and talks on the nuclear programme would start on the seventh day, he said.

This would include a protocol to allow UN nuclear inspectors back in to look at Iran’s damaged sites and the stockpile of highly enriched uranium.

Related: Trump faces tough choices as Iran dangles deal to reopen Hormuz before US midterms

Reports of the rejection came as Iranian state media reported on Saturday morning that Pezeshkian was on his way back to Tehran from New York.

The US president was earlier said to be privately sceptical Iran would meet his demands to dismantle its nuclear programme, according to unnamed US officials cited by the Wall Street Journal.

Trump has told aides he expects to resume bombing Iran after the November midterms in the US, the newspaper reported.

Meanwhile, on Friday evening, he published a post on his Truth Social platform with a graphic showing a map with the strait of Hormuz renamed as the “Trump Strait”.

The US naval blockade is putting intense pressure on the Iranian economy, while the seven-month-old conflict in the region has disrupted oil flows through one of the world’s most critical shipping lanes and is increasing the cost of living around the globe.

Previous attempts at diplomacy have failed to end the war, which began on 28 February with US and Israeli attacks.

Since then the conflict has alternated between pauses and renewed strikes, killing thousands while degrading Iran’s conventional forces and damaging its already ailing economy.

Iran and its allies have retaliated by extending the conflict throughout the region. Iran has struck US allies in the Gulf with drones and missiles while its Houthi allies in Yemen have targeted Saudi interests. Iranian-aligned militias in Iraq were blamed for a pipeline attack that temporarily took more Saudi oil off the market.

The violence in Yemen has prompted a new humanitarian crisis, the UN children’s agency said on Friday, reporting a rise in acute malnutrition among children.

Trump has previously said he was in no rush to reach a deal, even as high oil prices fuel inflation. On the Iranian side, there are questions as to whether the hardliners who dominate the security forces would accept compromises championed by moderates such as Pezeshkian.

Diplomatic efforts surrounding the UN general assembly underscored the global stakes in the conflict.

  • Marina Dunbar contributed. With Reuters and AP
output.standfirst: Iran says it remains ready to negotiate, despite distrust of Washington. Trump has rejected its offer to reopen the strait of Hormuz within a week and is said to expect renewed strikes after midterms.
output.progress: Iran's foreign minister says mediators are still expected to convey Washington's definitive response, after a US official earlier described the discussions as 'positive and constructive'.

output.headline: Family launches search fund to trace explorer Ranulph Fiennes
output.bodyHtml:
The stepson of Sir Ranulph Fiennes has launched a crowdfunder to pay for “specialist legal advice” to locate and safeguard the explorer, who has not been seen in public for more than two years.

Alexander Millington-Cotes, 31, has set a target of £55,000 for the fundraiser, to enable him to instruct lawyers to “locate and safeguard” Fiennes.

Millington-Cotes’ mother, Louise, from whom he is estranged, has lasting power of attorney in relation to Fiennes’ care, which her son wants to see revoked.

Friends and family are increasingly concerned for the welfare of the renowned expedition leader, who is 82 and has Parkinson’s disease.

It is understood that Louise, Fiennes’ second wife, has installed him in a succession of care homes where he has not been allowed to receive visitors.

According to the Telegraph, a watchdog concluded that his living arrangements amounted to a deprivation of his liberty because his wife had failed to ensure adequate legal safeguards were in place; the former soldier had previously spent time in a care home in Wales under a pseudonym.

The newspaper also said that Fiennes, widely considered the world’s greatest living explorer, had spent time in another care home in London, where visitors were apparently asked to sign non-disclosure agreements by Louise, 59, before being allowed to see him.

Arabella McIntyre-Brown, sister of Fiennes’ late first wife, Ginny, said she was so concerned about his welfare that she checked into the London home for a week in an attempt to speak to him. She told the Telegraph that he expressed a wish to see his friends.

Millington-Cotes’ crowdfunder had raised almost £3,000 on Saturday afternoon. He told supporters: “Ran has spent his entire life pushing boundaries for others and representing the best of human endurance. Now, he needs us to fight for him.”

He added that donations would cover “specialist legal representation and advice”, court fees and the cost of “determining [Fiennes’] exact location, to be shared with the relevant authorities”.

Millington-Cotes said he had a difficult relationship with his mother, who told him he was unwelcome at the family home two years ago.

About this time, Fiennes, the first person to cross Antarctica on foot, failed to appear at a gala evening organised in his honour at the Royal Geographical Society in Kensington, west London.

Instead, he delivered a brief, prerecorded message from home, saying he was “not well enough” to attend in person. He has not been seen publicly since.

Millington-Cotes alleged that he had been forced to visit his stepfather in secret after the breakdown of his relationship with his mother.

“Since being asked to leave the family home and not come back, I can only imagine the amplification of Ran’s difficulties and isolation,” he said.

“His isolation would consist of being effectively annexed in the other end of the house, with relatively minimal contact.

“I remember him gleaming the occasional times I would appear unannounced with some sweet treats, which I’d had to haul with me as I climbed over the seven-foot industrial entrance gate.

“The last time I saw Ran was when he whisked me away while I was walking up the drive on one of my infrequent visits, sadly neither him or I realised that it may be the last time we’d see and hug one another.

“This is the moment he told me he was proud of me, a sweet moment in my memory.”

He said that, over the past two years, he had “tried multiple avenues” in an effort to locate his stepfather, whom his mother married in 2005.

Ginny, to whom Fiennes was married for 34 years, had died of cancer the previous year. Louise gave birth to a daughter, Elizabeth, in 2006, Fiennes’ only biological child.

Related: Explorer review – compelling portrait of adventurer Ranulph Fiennes

While Millington-Cotes described his stepfather as “a man of immense heart, kindness, and selflessness who supported me for years”, he said his strained relationship with Louise had caused him “great pain and distress”.

“Upon learning from other friends and family that Ran was considered missing, I put aside my own pain and immediately felt anger,” he said. “Anger that similar experiences I’d had were now being cast on to Ran. A man for as long as I could remember was completely selfless, kind and abided by an excellent moral code.”

He added that he had visited various care homes hoping to find Fiennes “to have a simple conversation with him, or to be able to take him for a brief coffee”, but had so far been unsuccessful and had “left with a feeling of dismay and a slightly emptier heart.”

Millington-Cotes said that any excess funds would be donated to Marie Curie and the British Heart Foundation, favoured charities of Fiennes.
output.standfirst: Alexander Millington-Cotes has launched a £55,000 crowdfunder to locate and safeguard his stepfather, explorer Sir Ranulph Fiennes, 82, who has not been seen in public for two years amid concerns for his welfare.
output.progress: Alexander Millington-Cotes has launched a £55,000 crowdfunder for legal help, which had raised almost £3,000 by Saturday afternoon.

output.headline: Bellingham drives England fightback against world champions Spain
output.bodyHtml:
Thomas Tuchel's England met defeat with none of the recriminations of last time, even as they let a second-half lead slip and lost 3-2 to Spain. The England support can accept losing when their team plays with cut and thrust, and, more to the point, they can accept losing to a Spain side who, at times, played football from a different stratosphere.

Jude Bellingham drove England on, running on adrenaline and playing to the point of maximum expression. England were game throughout and had positive surges either side of the interval, none better than the one towards the end of the first half, when goals from Anthony Gordon and Harry Kane put them 2-1 up, hauling them back after Lamine Yamal’s second-minute goal.

Related: Thomas Tuchel denies England players were distracted by Manchester City verdict

England did well to stay within a puncher’s chance of a result in this Nations League opener, and Bellingham was still driving them forward in stoppage time. Crucially, as Tuchel and England look to move on from the heartbreak of the World Cup semi-final defeat against Argentina, there was no negativity from the Wembley crowd, even in the face of defending that was dreadfully loose. The biggest takeaway, though, was Spain’s slickness: there is a reason why they won the World Cup in the summer and the European Championship before that. They are the best team in the international game by a distance, and nobody can live with them.

There were none of the dreaded boos at the full-time whistle. Earlier, in the countdown to kick-off, the reaction to Tuchel’s name went untested: after the starting XI and the 12 substitutes were read out, his name was not announced with the team.

Spain had been the better side for the opening 30 minutes, and when they went again after the Kane penalty, they had too much for England. The match turned on that penalty miss in the 54th minute: had the captain scored, rather than hitting the crossbar after his standing foot gave way in the turf, England would have been 3-1 up. Instead, they were pegged back to 2-2 by the Spain substitute Álex Baena, and there was a degree of inevitability about the winner from another replacement, Mikel Oyarzabal, whose dinked finish was impudently brilliant. It was a statement of intent from Spain, an illustration of their remorseless desire.

“Campeones” was the chant from the enclosure housing the travelling fans before kick-off, and it is fair to say the visiting radio commentators were excited about seeing Spain for the first time since the second star was stitched on to their shirt. Their fervour went up a few notches in the early running when Lamine Yamal opened the scoring.

The goal was a personal disaster for Marc Guéhi; it was almost as if the Manchester City defender had other things on his mind. It was of a piece with England’s struggles against the Spanish press. Guéhi was facing upfield as he tried to build a move from deep but his passing lanes were blocked. So he checked back and walked straight into Lamine Yamal, who robbed him and was clean through. He made the finish past James Trafford look easy.

Trafford has been outstanding for Leeds since joining them over the summer, and he heard the knock of opportunity when Tuchel started him ahead of Jordan Pickford, a major deviation from the head coach’s stated intention for continuity from the World Cup. Pickford had been erratic in the summer and was punished for some of his mistakes. Tuchel’s plan is to share the goalkeeping minutes between Trafford and Pickford during this window, and Trafford repaid the trust by helping to keep England in the game as Spain pushed to add to Lamine Yamal’s goal.

Related: Meet the new 55 minute England collapse, not the same as the old 55 minute England collapse | Barney Ronay

Spain kept pushing. They shimmered with menace, with the movement, the speed of it and the breathtaking assurance on the ball meaning they had so many options in possession that it felt at times as if they had more men on the pitch.

Trafford stood up to make a big one-on-one save from the Spain striker after Lamine Yamal had played the through-ball, while at the other end Ferran Torres had already had the ball in the net, only for it to be ruled out for offside. England’s backline was all over the place, but Trafford made himself big once more when Torres blew another one-on-one chance on 28 minutes, and Dani Olmo rifled just wide after a sumptuous Lamine Yamal flick.

England’s resistance was impressive as they tried to throw counterpunches while hanging on, with Gordon and Bellingham to the fore. They showed their personality when the chips were down, and when the two combined for an equaliser that had not really been advertised, it prompted a wild turnaround.

Spain were pushing again when Nico Williams lost his footing and the ball fell to Elliot Anderson. England swept forward in thrilling style, Gordon flicking to Bellingham, who got the ball back and surged in on goal; the low finish was nerveless.

Kane had his moments: unlucky when he banged a shot inches wide from the edge of the area after a Bukayo Saka burst, then lucky when his header from a Nico O’Reilly cross, which Unai Simón looked to have covered, drew a panicked reaction from Marc Cucurella. The left-back jutted out his thigh and turned the ball past his own goalkeeper. The fates were against Cucurella again when his mishit cross on 45 minutes sailed over Trafford and came back off the far post.

Bellingham appeared particularly determined to leave his imprint. The Real Madrid midfielder was in the mood for bragging rights back in La Liga. It was the power and directness of his running; the smoothness of it, the quickness of his moves. Spain could not contain him. It was his persistence after yet another surge that led to the penalty.

Gordon played the pass back inside from the left and Bellingham got there before Rodri, who invited trouble when he hung out a leg. Down went Bellingham and after a review, it was decided that the contact trumped the feeling that the England player had tried to engineer it. Kane could not convert.

Back came Spain. Lamine Yamal pushed a shot wide after a give and go with Baena, whose backheel was beautiful. Then Baena equalised after O’Reilly gave away the ball and Olmo quickly shifted it to the edge of the area. Baena bought himself the space for the shot with an expert drop of the shoulder.

Saka curled just wide at the other end after more good work by Bellingham but the tide had turned. You could not take your eyes off Lamine Yamal while Luis de la Fuente’s attack-minded changes worked. It was Oyarzabal who made the difference from a Baena pass. England could have no complaints.
output.standfirst: Jude Bellingham drove a spirited England fightback and James Trafford excelled in goal, but Harry Kane’s missed penalty proved pivotal as Spain, the world champions, won 3-2 at Wembley.
output.progress: Thomas Tuchel is rotating James Trafford and Jordan Pickford in goal this window, and Trafford repaid the trust by helping keep England in the game.

output.headline: Mass protests push Spain’s government to promise swift housing reforms
output.bodyHtml:
Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, promised on Wednesday to swiftly introduce a raft of housing measures. “Maricarmen’s eviction is a social tragedy that we cannot accept,” he said, after the 87-year-old woman was evicted from her home. Sánchez now faces questions over whether his government has done enough to make good on its promise to make housing a priority.

Images of the 87-year-old being evicted from the home she had lived in for seven decades on a stretcher, flanked by protesters and police officers, sparked indignation across Spain.

Hours later, people began taking to the streets. In Madrid, an estimated 10,000 people turned up on Wednesday, wielding signs that read “Shame” and “Out with the vulture funds”, to protest against the eviction of Maricarmen Abascal. From the northern tip of Spain to the south, people poured into plazas calling for a nationwide reckoning over access to housing.

Related: Police use teargas on protesters as disabled woman, 87, evicted from Madrid home

The catalyst was the eviction of Abascal, now known across the country by her first name, Maricarmen. The 87-year-old woman with a disability said she had been forced to leave her home after she was unable to afford the 230% rent hike demanded by the investment fund that bought her apartment.

“This eviction is the canary in the coalmine,” said political scientist Cristina Monge. “It’s become a symbol, seen as the tip of the iceberg when it comes to the issue of housing.”

It was, as newspaper El País said in an editorial, a glimpse of a housing market that had become completely unmoored from the average income in Spain, as rents rose 80% in a decade, while the cost of homes had climbed by 63%. “The law was upheld, and the market worked. But it is the law of the jungle in a broken market, and it is a failure.”

The investment fund linked to the eviction of Maricarmen did not reply to a request for comment from the Guardian.

Saturday saw around 25,000 people, according to government figures, take to the streets of Madrid, rattling keys as they called for measures to curb rising housing costs and make evictions more difficult. Some brought tents and sleeping bags, announcing plans to set up a protest camp in Madrid’s central Sol plaza.

The eviction had left many in Spain grappling with a sense of “powerlessness”, said Monge, given that the issue of housing had also been at the forefront of the Spanish Indignados movement, or 15-M, the years-long anti-austerity and anti-corruption protest movement that involved millions of Spaniards and reshaped the country’s politics.

“Now, 15 years later, housing is still the number one concern of Spaniards. And there are still evictions every day, to the order of about 25,000 per year,” she said. “But the paradox is that the country’s government includes some of the same people who led the 15-M protests. And still, housing remains an enormous challenge.”

Rights campaigners and researchers weighed in this week with potential solutions, citing the more than 3m homes believed to be sitting empty across the country, and government figures that suggest social housing makes up just 2.5% of the total stock in Spain, compared to 14% in France and 34% in the Netherlands, even as politicians laid the blame on each other for the eviction.

The head of one of the country’s biggest labour unions called for investment funds to be “kicked out” of the housing market. “Homes are for living in, not for large corporations to do business,” said Unai Sordo of the Workers’ Commissions (CCOO) as he called for a tax system that would make “the business of hoarding homes unprofitable”.

The UN’s special rapporteur on the right to housing, Koldo Casla, called on Spain to amend the laws governing its legal system, describing it as “impossible to understand” how the profitability of a real estate company had been prioritised over Maricarmen’s right to housing.

The leftwing coalition Sumar, the junior partner in the government, said it would push the socialist-led government to greenlight the expropriation of Maricarmen’s former home as well as put forward a package of rent freezes.

The widespread demand for change has cast a spotlight on the deep divisions that exist among Spain’s political parties when it comes to the issue of housing. These divisions were laid bare earlier this year when the conservative People’s party, the far-right Vox and the hardline Catalan pro-independence party Junts voted to end a moratorium on evictions that for six years had managed to shield some vulnerable tenants from eviction.

While the Sánchez government had in 2023 managed to pass legislation that strengthened tenant protection and widened access to rent control, regions led by the People’s party had wielded their powers over housing to avoid implementing parts of the legislation.

Among those who had ignored parts of the legislation was the rightwing leader of the Madrid region, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, who in recent weeks has faced questions over her administration’s decision to allegedly spend €6.3m (£5.4m) of public funds on a residential penthouse to use as a temporary office.

The striking contrast between the allegations against Ayuso and the eviction of Maricarmen has repeatedly cropped up this week, from the decision to hold Wednesday’s protest in Madrid on a boulevard next to the penthouse, to the chants urging “Ayuso’s penthouse for Maricarmen”.

The regional leader has so far sought to downplay the significance of Maricarmen’s eviction, describing it as “one out of the 25,500 that take place every year in Spain” and noting that it had been authorised by the country’s courts.

While the story of Maricarmen had dominated headlines, turning the octogenarian into the poster woman for those bearing the brunt of Spain’s soaring real estate market, many pointed to her plight as a glimpse of a wider reality.

“Maricarmen’s case is not an isolated incident; it is just one more example of the suffering endured by thousands of households in Spain,” Amnesty International Spain said in a statement. “Bold measures must be taken immediately. Institutions must go beyond simply expressing regret in the press, they must take action.”
output.standfirst: Tens of thousands rallied across Spain and Pedro Sánchez pledged swift housing reforms after 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal was evicted when she could not afford a 230% rent rise imposed by an investment fund.

output.headline: Widespread support carries NAZA film-makers to New York premiere
output.bodyHtml:
The film-makers behind NAZA, the award-winning documentary on Israel’s systemic mass killing of Palestinians in Gaza, brought the film to its North American premiere in New York on Saturday and defended their findings, even as Israeli officials escalate threats to strip them of their citizenship amid protests in Israel.

The critically acclaimed film, directed by Oscar-winning film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor and produced by the Guardian, features the testimony of 24 anonymized Israeli soldiers and intelligence officers involved in the surveillance and remote killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza, who describe the AI-powered systems used to select their targets. The project takes its name from an acronym used euphemistically by Israeli intelligence to indicate how many civilians it expects to die in an airstrike, which are often conducted at night in private homes, killing many family members, including children, at once.

‘Our country is doing so much to hide these systems,’ Szor told the audience at the New York film festival in a Q&A that followed the film’s premiere. ‘It’s not a world that is open even to the Israeli public.’

‘These crimes that you saw are ongoing,’ Abraham said. ‘They’re ongoing because it’s what our country is doing, and because of what your country is supporting and funding.’

The 80-minute documentary, filmed in secret on rooftops in Tel Aviv, builds on reporting published from 2023 to 2025 in the Guardian; +972 Magazine, an Israeli-Palestinian publication; and Hebrew-language outlet Local Call. It held its world premiere earlier this month at the Venice film festival, where it received a 25-minute standing ovation – a festival record – and went on to win the special jury prize.

More than 1,500 Israeli film professionals, 43 Israeli human rights organizations and the directors of major international festivals have defended Abraham and Szor, as have numerous international press freedom organizations. The film is currently set for release next month in cinemas in 55 countries, before a digital global release, for free, on the Guardian’s website in November, as part of the organization’s commitment to the dissemination of independent journalism.

The film has been met with fierce derision from Israeli officials as well as threats to the film-makers, amid a tense election season largely focused on Benjamin Netanyahu’s ongoing campaign in Gaza, which has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians to date and has been declared a genocide by numerous international agencies, including the United Nations.

A couple dozen protesters gathered outside the film’s premiere at the Lincoln Center on Saturday afternoon, brandishing Israeli flags and signs calling for viewers to ‘learn the facts’ of the 7 October 2023 attacks by Hamas on Israeli civilians. At least one truck with LED screens accusing NAZA of being ‘propaganda dressed up as a documentary’ circled the theater.

NAZA’s New York City premiere came just a day after the Israeli prime minister offered an aggressive defense of Israel’s use of deadly force in Gaza just across Central Park to the UN general assembly. As hundreds of protesters gathered outside and dozens of diplomats inside walked out in solidarity with Palestinians, Netanyahu called Israel’s war in Gaza the ‘opposite of genocide’ and denounced Israel’s critics. Netanyahu had previously said he would seek new laws to strip citizenship from people who ‘smear’ Israeli soldiers in response to NAZA.

‘So, to all those spreading these lies about my country and about our brave soldiers, whether they sit in this hall or in the office of the antisemitic mayor of New York, I say this: shame on you!’ he said Thursday.

On Friday, Netanyahu reiterated his plan to advance legislation revoking the citizenship of Abraham and Szor, two of the four film-makers behind No Other Land, an unstinting look at the Israeli-occupied West Bank, which won the Oscar for best documentary in 2025. In an interview with the conservative Israeli outlet Makor Rishon, he likened NAZA to ‘launching dozens of ballistic missiles’ at Israel.

Abraham addressed the missile comment directly in the post-screening Q&A, referring to such a characterization as ‘the criminalization of journalism and of this kind of work’.

He also defended the film’s use of anonymous sources as necessary to expose systems of mass killing hidden by the Israeli state. ‘Throughout the history of investigative journalism, very often granting confidentiality to sources is a means to pursue the truth,’ he said. ‘This film could not have been made any other way and because the crimes are ongoing, we felt that it was important to make it.’

Along with Netanyahu, Israel’s culture minister, Miki Zohar, has called for the film-makers’ citizenship to be revoked, and accused them of ‘treason against the state’. The IDF’s chief of staff, Eyal Zamir, said the military would ‘not allow IDF soldiers to be made targets through lies and blood libels’ and would use ‘every tool at our disposal’ against the film.

Rightwing activists have gone even further, calling for violence against the pair. Earlier this month, dozens of agitators surrounded Szor’s parents’ home in central Israel, with one protester calling for the ‘death penalty for traitors’.

But the US premiere Saturday held particular resonance, given the country’s annual $3.8bn in military assistance to Israel – a connection the film-makers noted to the New York City crowd.

‘These soldiers are talking about what has been done with the taxpayer money of the people sitting here,’ said Abraham.

He also responded to the protesters outside the theater invoking the attacks of October 7. ‘It’s in the film and it’s completely unjustified,’ he said of the massacre, which killed 1,200 Israelis, most of them civilians. ‘But it also cannot justify what you’ve seen in the film. It doesn’t justify the slaughter of so many civilians in Gaza.’

‘I don’t want to live in a world where rightful empathy to Israeli victims is weaponized by leaders like Netanyahu – cynical people who promise nothing other than perpetual occupation and war,’ he added. ‘It’s weaponized to mean a lack of empathy to Palestinians, to mean this continuous killing and murder of people. I don’t think we should want to live in such a world. I think we should all refuse to play this zero-sum game.’
output.standfirst: Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor’s documentary on Israel’s killing of Palestinians in Gaza reached New York backed by widespread industry support, even as Israeli officials threaten to strip the film-makers of their citizenship.

output.headline: 700,000 gather in Paris for pope's first visit to France in 18 years
output.bodyHtml:
The Vatican estimated that 700,000 people turned out for an open-air mass with Pope Leo in Paris on Saturday – about 100,000 more than the number of people who had registered to attend.

Hundreds of thousands of people lined the Avenue des Champs-Élysées to attend the mass, on the second day of the pope’s visit to France.

It is the first official papal visit to France in 18 years.

Cheers rang out in the crowd as the pope thanked God in his homily for the chance to visit France on a whirlwind four-day, three-city tour to promote Catholicism and its teachings.

The mass took place at the Place de la Concorde, the site of bloody executions by guillotine during the French Revolution – when Louis XVI’s staunchly Catholic rule was overthrown – and now the centre of the secular republic.

The choice of the site, a symbol of the French republic to many, was criticised by supporters of France’s strict legislation separating church and state in public life.

Pope Leo asked those in the crowd not to keep their faith to themselves. “Let it overflow, so that those you meet may be refreshed and their thirst satisfied,” he said. “From this beautiful city of Paris, I pray fervently that the living water of the Holy Spirit may flow throughout France.”

He told Catholics that only their faith, and not material things, can provide true happiness.

“Only God can fill the emptiness within us,” he said.

Chanting “Leo, Leo” and “Long live the pope”, crowds of people waved French and Vatican flags as the pontiff rode slowly down the grand boulevard of the Champs-Élysées aboard a popemobile – a specially designed, partly open vehicle used during public appearances.

He stopped frequently along the way as babies were lifted out of the crowd and brought to him to receive a papal caress on their heads. The city centre was sealed off for the service, with helicopters circling overhead and snipers positioned on rooftops.

The security zone for the event – the biggest of the papal tour – stretched about 1.4 miles (2.2km), shutting down road traffic in central Paris from the Place de la Concorde to the Arc de Triomphe and beyond.

About 14,500 police officers, gendarmes, military personnel and firefighters were deployed to the event, which was attended by 2,400 priests and deacons, and about 100 bishops.

Marie-Élisabeth, a 44-year-old nun from Burgundy, told a reporter for France 24: “This event is a way for us to say loud and proud that Christians are here.”

Speaking to reporters from Agence France-Presse, Sylvie Leclerc, a 51-year-old teacher, also said she and her fellow Christians want to share their fervour for their faith. “You don’t hear much from us Catholics, but now we’re going to make some noise!” she said. “But to proclaim love, peace, joy.”
output.standfirst: Some 700,000 people, 100,000 more than registered, packed Paris for Pope Leo’s mass on his first French visit in 18 years, though supporters of France’s separation of church and state criticised the venue.
output.progress: French authorities deployed 14,500 police, gendarmes, military personnel and firefighters to secure the mass safely.
